newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan plans neighbours' Afghan peace meeting.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan plans neighbours' Afghan peace meeting.

text.p: Pakistan said on Thursday it was planning to host a conference of five immediate neighbours of war-shattered Afghanistan to discuss ways to end the prolonged conflict there.

Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan told a news conference that the meeting would involve Iran, Pakistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and that the United States and Russia might attend as observers.

Khan said he would make a two-day tour to Central Asian countries neighbouring Afghanistan next week to discuss the conference plan while Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif would also discuss the subject with Iranian leaders when he visits Tehran on June 16-17.
Dates for the conference would be set in consultation with other participating countries.
Khan said Pakistan was also trying to hold an intra-Afghan dialogue under U.N. auspices with the aim of having a broad-based government in the war-shattered country.
Pakistan recognised the government of the Taleban Islamic movement in Afghanistan late last month, a move followed by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
It is accused by opposition factions of helping the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, which control more than two-thirds of Afghanistan.
Pakistan denies the charge, and Khan said all ethnic groups should take part in the intra-Afghan dialogue "so that a broad-based government is formed".

Khan said the Taleban qualified for recognition because the militia controlled 22 of Afghanistan's 32 provinces and the capital Kabul while nobody knew where the ousted government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani, which still occupies the country's seat at the United Nations, was holding its meetings.
"A lot of Western countries do say that...the world will not accept the Taleban or Pashtuns to rule the whole of Afghanistan," Khan said.
"That has never been so. Whoever has been in government in Kabul or in Afghanistan has had all the various ethnic groups in the government."
Khan said "new ground realities" and new leadership had emerged in Afghanistan and outside powers could not force rulers on Afghanistan whom people there did not like.

"The British tried it, the Russians tried it," he said referring to the British efforts to dominate Afghanistan earlier this century and the Soviet intervention in the 1980s. "Whoever has tried it has failed," Khan said. "It doesn't fit into the Afghan psyche or into the Afghan society.
